Hetzron (1969, 1997) reported a penultimate demarcative stress feature operating independently from tone. I am not able to confirm this observation. How tone and stress relate to each other in Awngi will be explored in section 4." | p.22: "Both characteristics are incompatible with an interpretation of tone as being merely a manifestation of a stress feature" | fn.32 p.22: "In any case, I found no evidence in the varieties of Awngi which I have studied of the “weak stress of intensity” attested by Hetzron (1978:123) on the penultimate syllable." ||| Hetzron 1976 p.42 (scanned, transcriptions garbled): "Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every deciding passage (Joswig 2010 p.3, p.22, fn.32; Hetzron 1976 p.42) is verbatim in the held files at the stated locators; only Hetzron 1969 p.7 is carried, and the record says so. The classification 'conflict' rests on the latest dedicated phonology (Joswig 2010, SIL EWP, publisher PDF) against Hetzron's repeated penult-stress claim (1969/1976/1978/1997), which is the right pairing given Glottolog's list: the only 'grammar' (Yaregal 2016) is of the Kunfäl dialect and, fetched sources and read today, is tone-only and silent on stress; the other listed phonology (Worku 1986 MA, fetched sources today) gives yet another stress account — predictable, non-phonemic, word-INITIAL by default and word-FINAL for polysyllabic adjectives/adverbs/imperatives, under four tone levels — which agrees with neither Hetzron's penult nor Joswig's 'no evidence'. sources.quote: 'We can observe that stress is placed either on the first syllable or on the final syllable' (p.56); rule: stress on the first syllable by default; 'if the word is polysyllabic and together with the grammatical category it belongs [adjective, adverb, or imperative], its final syllable will be stressed' (p.57); 'Thus, if stress is predictable, we can conclude it is nonphonemic (or fixed) in Awngi' (p.57); final stress 'is accompanied by the concomitant lengthening (fortition) of the onset consonant' (p.58). Summary p.63: 'five suprasegments (a stress and four tone levels) ... two tonemes'. Exam
sources.locator: ch.4 'Suprasegmentals', sec. 4.1 'Stress and Length', printed pp.55-58 (PDF pp.64-67); Summary p.63
sources.note: Third primary on Awngi prosody, not in the record: gives predictable non-phonemic stress on the FIRST syllable (final for polysyllabic adjectives/adverbs/imperatives) alongside four tone levels — a location incompatible with Hetzron's penult, reinforcing the conflict verdict; should be added to prule/contra.

sources.citation: Yaregal Allene Teferra. 2016. A Grammar of Kulazngi. PhD dissertation, Addis Ababa University (438 pp; Kulazngi = the Kunfäl/Kulisi variety, which the author classes as a dialect of Awngi, p.1329-1330 of text). Glottolog ref 568202. AAU ETD item 5db64caa-9d75-4cf6-986a-ac1292c8110b.
sources.quote: 'By all definitions above, Kulazngi is a tone language, or it is not a mere pitch-accent language, because every syllable in a word bears low, mid, or high tone having a lexical as well as a grammatical function' (p.44); 'Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones' (p.45). No word-stress statement anywhere in the phonology chapter (only mention of stress: 'Kemanteney has only stress (Hetzron 1976)'); no penultimate/initial prominence rule given.
sources.note: Glottolog's only 'grammar' for awng1244 (Kunfäl/Kulisi dialect); its phonology chapter describes H/M/L + HL tone with lexical and grammatical function and gives no word-stress rule — silent on stress, consistent with Joswig's tone-only analysis.
